title: A server that grants a vote without adopting the candidate's term elects two leaders
summary: A Raft server that receives a vote request from a newer term adopts the term and becomes a follower of it, and only then applies the vote rule. A developer stops the adoption, so that a server whose timer fired cannot drag the cluster into a new term by asking: the vote rule already counts a candidate's newer term as a free vote, so the vote is still granted. The contract diff is three cases, one per role, and is approved; the vote rule is untouched and its regression proofs pass. The election model finds a five-step run that ends with two leaders in one term.

change.description: On a `RequestVote` from a newer term, answer `unchanged` instead of `transition(FOLLOWER, ADOPT_TERM)`. The reasoning in the comment: a server adopts a term when it hears from a leader; a mere request for votes should not move it, because a server that keeps timing out, partitioned or slow, raises the whole cluster's term every time it asks (the disruptive server of Ongaro's thesis, section 4.2.3). The vote rule, `VoteRule.grant`, treats a candidate's term that is ahead of the voter's as a free vote, so the candidate still gets it. The behavioural contract is regenerated and its diff is the three cases `decide(FOLLOWER | CANDIDATE | LEADER, RequestVote[term=NEWER])`, from a transition with `ADOPT_TERM` to unchanged; a test for the new rule is added. The reviewer approves the diff.

risk: The vote rule's `candidateTerm > currentTerm` clause is not a second way to grant a vote; it is the first half of a rule whose second half is that the voter then has that term, with its vote recorded in it. Without the adoption, the voter stays in its old term with no vote recorded in the new one, and the next candidate of the same term is also ahead of it, also free, also granted. One server votes twice in one term, two candidates each reach a majority with it, and two leaders serve the same term: the election safety property of Raft (figure 3), on which every other guarantee rests, is gone. Each leader appends entries at the same indexes; whichever one the clients reach, committed entries are overwritten. The role machine's contract is exactly what the developer intended, and the vote rule's proofs pass, because the vote rule did not change: the failure is in how the two kernels compose, which neither contract states.
explanation: The election model has one action per RPC of a server, with the role transitions generated from the behavioural contract of `RoleMachine#decide`, which the tool proves the bytecode satisfies on all 52 inputs, and the vote rule written as `VoteRule.grant` is, without the log comparison. TLC checks every interleaving of three servers over three terms. With the committed rule every invariant and both action properties hold in all 610 states. With the patched rule it reports the shortest run that breaks `ElectionSafety`: s1's timer fires and it runs for term 1; s2's fires and it runs for term 1 too; s1 asks s3, which is in term 0, grants, records the vote and stays in term 0, and s1 has a majority; s2 asks s3, whose term is still behind s2's, so the vote is free again, and s2 has a majority. Two leaders in term 1, in five steps. The trace shows the state that makes it possible, `votedFor = s1` on a server whose `currentTerm` is still 0, a combination the committed rule never produces. The model's candidate counts the granted reply, as a server that trusts the reply does; a server that discarded a reply from an older term would never elect a leader at all under this rule, which is the other way the change breaks the cluster.
resolution: Revert. The rule in the paper (figure 2, rules for all servers) is unconditional: any RPC with a term ahead of the server's makes it a follower of that term, requests included, and the vote rule is stated for a voter that is already in the candidate's term. The disruptive-server problem the developer meant to solve has its own fix, the pre-vote phase of section 4.2.3, in which a server asks whether it could win before it increments its term; that keeps the adoption rule intact. The election model stays in the build, so that the next change to the role machine is checked against what the vote rule assumes of it.
provenance: Constructed from the rules for all servers in figure 2 of the Raft paper, by removing the term adoption from the handling of RequestVote.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (2014): section 5.2, leader election, and figure 3, election safety
Ongaro, Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice (2014): chapter 3, the basic algorithm, and section 4.2.3, disruptive servers
